[00:00] Welcome to lecture eight. We've been designing agents and extending co-pilots throughout this section. Now we tackle the advanced extensibility mechanisms that let agents [music] reach beyond their built-in capabilities. Model context protocol or MCP is how agents securely access external tools. UI automation and RPA lets agents control UIs for legacy systems. And agent behaviors like reasoning and voice mode expand what agents can do. These are all specifically called out in the exam, so let's cover those. MCP solves a critical problem. Without it, agents called APIs directly. The agent has the API key.

[00:47] The agent might leak that. There's no audit trail and it doesn't scale. MCP adds a middleman. Instead of calling Dynamics 365 directly, the agent says, "MCP, give me the email for customer ID 12345." MCP checks permissions, validates input, enforces rate limits, forwards to the actual service, and logs the entire interaction. There are three advantages to this. Security. Agents never see API keys.

[01:21] Auditability. Every request is logged with user context and timestamp. Interoperability. Multiple agents across Co-pilot Studio, Foundry, and custom apps share the same tools. Here's the practical design guidance. Register tools as MCP servers in Azure. Standardize your tool schemas so that any agent can call them. Use context passing with A2A to share session state when agents hand off work.

[01:53] On the exam, when you see "securely integrate with a legacy system" or "ensure compliance with full traceability", MCP is almost always part of that answer. Now, MCP isn't the only option. Co-pilot Studio also supports REST API tools and skills. REST API tools let you define custom HTTP endpoints with an open API spec. It's simpler than MCP when you need a single integration. Skills are pre-built AI building blocks for common tasks like entity extraction or summarization. So, the exam decision is this: simple direct API access for one agent, so use the REST API tool.

[02:42] Secure, shared, auditable across multiple agents, MCP. Now, UI automation and RPA is an emerging capability that lets agents interact with user interfaces directly. Instead of calling APIs, the agent reads the screen, clicks buttons, types in the fields, and parses results. The use case is the legacy system automation.

[03:10] Organizations with 20-year-old applications that have no API, without UI automation and RPA, a human enters data manually. With RPA and UI automation, the agent handles the form filling. But it's risky. The agent can misclick or type wrong data. So, guardrails are essential. You have to whitelist specific actions, require user confirmation before sensitive operations, and define timeouts so a stuck agent doesn't loop forever. So, your exam principle, MCP when APIs exist, UI automation and RPA only when there's no API, and always with strict controls.

[03:57] Beyond MCP and UI automation and RPA, the exam tests several specific agent behaviors you can configure in Co-pilot Studio. Reasoning mode uses chain of thought processing for multi-step problems. The agent reasons step-by-step. Check the account, calculate the discount eligibility, verify inventory, and then provide the final price. It's more accurate for complex scenarios, but higher latency, takes longer.

[04:30] So, here's a design consideration. Show a progress indicator so the user isn't staring at a blank screen. Voice mode enables spoken interaction over the phone or Teams audio. This is important for customer service and field workers where typing isn't practical. The key constraint is latency. A 2-second pause in text is fine, but in voice, it's awkward. Also, voice transcription produces variations, so the agent needs to be able to handle those. Now, autonomous triggers let an agent act on events without a user prompt. A supply chain agent that detects a stockout and auto triggers a reorder. We talked about that before. The design requirement, confidence thresholds and escalation rules because autonomous actions happen

[05:23] without a human in the loop. Generative answers are the fallback when no topic matches. The agent uses the language model to generate the response. This must be grounded. Ungrounded generative answers are where hallucinations come from. In Co-pilot Studio, you configure which knowledge sources generative answers can pull from from. So, here are your key takeaways. Number one, MCP enables secure, auditable tool access. Register tools as MCP servers. Agents never see API keys and every call is logged with user context. For a simpler scenario, REST API tools and skills offer lighter-weight alternatives. Number two,
